opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting tensions in the field right now. AI research is fundamentally empirical. We don't have a strong theory that tells us, before training a model, what it will be able to do or why a particular architectural choice will work. So progress comes from running experiments, a lot of them, and seeing what happens.

But you can't run every experiment. Compute is expensive and the space of possible ideas is huge. That's where intuition comes in. The researchers who seem to have outsized impact are often the ones with a really good sense of which experiments are worth running. They look at a loss curve or a weird model behavior and think, "That's interesting, let's pull on that thread." A lot of that taste comes from having run thousands of experiments and built an internal model of how these systems behave, even if they can't fully articulate it.

I don't think it's magic, though. Intuition is compressed experience. It's built by iterating quickly, being wrong a lot, and paying close attention to why you were wrong. That's why fast experimental infrastructure matters so much. The faster your feedback loop, the faster you build good intuitions.

From an interpretability perspective, which is where I spend a lot of my time, I see this as both a strength and a limitation. Relying on intuition works, but it's hard to transfer, hard to verify, and it can lead the field to over-index on a few people's hunches. Part of the goal of interpretability is to turn some of that tacit knowledge into something more scientific: actually understanding the mechanisms inside these models, so we can make predictions instead of just relying on gut feeling.

So my view is that experimentation and intuition reinforce each other right now, and that's fine for an early-stage science. But in the long run, I'd like the field to move toward deeper understanding, where intuition is guided by real theory and not just pattern-matching from experience.

r003.rationale: It says interpretability can help understand model mechanisms, but does not specifically connect that understanding to why some AI methods succeed and others fail.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's worth being honest that AI research right now is a deeply empirical field. We don't have a theory that tells us, from first principles, why a given architecture or training recipe works. So almost everything we know, we know because someone tried it and it either worked or didn't. That's not a criticism, it's just where the science is. Chemistry looked like this before we understood the atom.

Given that, intuition is basically compressed experimentation. The researchers people describe as having "great taste" are usually the ones who've run an enormous number of experiments, personally, and internalized which ideas tend to survive contact with scale and which don't. It feels like magic from the outside, but it's mostly pattern matching on a very large private dataset of failures. The more hands-on you've been, the better calibrated your priors get.

The dependence on that does worry me in a couple of ways, though. One is that it concentrates the ability to do frontier research in a small number of people and labs with the compute to build that intuition. If the only way to learn what works is to run thousands of experiments at scale, most academics can't participate in that loop, and their intuitions drift away from what actually matters at the frontier.

The other is that intuition doesn't transfer well. If someone just "knows" an idea won't work and can't articulate why, we can't teach it, we can't audit it, and we can't tell when it's gone stale. A lot of my own interest in interpretability comes from this. If we understood mechanistically what models are doing, some of what's currently tacit knowledge could become actual explanations. I don't think experimentation goes away, but I'd like the field to move toward a place where strong intuition is the starting hypothesis rather than the final authority.

astra-6.text:
I think AI research is still very empirical. We have useful theories, but they often don’t tell you which approach will work best at scale. So you run experiments, look at what happened, and revise your understanding.

That makes intuition valuable, because the space of possible experiments is enormous. A researcher with good intuition can pick a question or notice a result that other people might overlook. But I wouldn’t treat that intuition as something magical. A lot of it comes from spending time with models, seeing things fail, and developing a sense of which details matter.

The important thing is that intuition should generate hypotheses, and experiments should test them. If we rely entirely on a few unusually insightful people, progress becomes hard to reproduce. Ideally, their discoveries give us explanations and methods that let everyone else reason more effectively, too.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI research is still very empirical. You have an idea, you run an experiment, and the result often surprises you. We have useful theories, but they don’t yet tell us reliably which changes will work at scale. So experimentation is part of how we build understanding.

That makes intuition valuable, because the space of possible experiments is enormous. A strong researcher can look at a result and ask, “What’s the most informative thing to try next?” Sometimes that means spotting an opportunity; sometimes it means realizing that an exciting result is probably a bug.

But intuition has to be tested. Ideally, you turn a hunch into a clear hypothesis, run a controlled experiment, and update your view when the evidence disagrees. The goal should be to turn individual insights into knowledge other people can use, so progress depends less on a few unusually intuitive researchers.
